newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Motorola woes don't worry European cellphone firms.
newsitem.headline: Motorola woes don't worry European cellphone firms.

text.p: STOCKHOLM, Sept 12 - Key players in Europe's mobile phone market remain confident about market share in the short term despite a bleak outlook from U.S. rival Motorola, on , but the future looks less certain, analysts said on Thursday.

Motorola Inc, the world's mobile phone titan, warned on Wednesday that its third quarter profits would be significantly lower than expected earlier, partly due to a slide in international mobile phone sales over the past two months.
The weak outlook shocked the market and knocked the share prices of some European rivals such as Nokia, Ericsson, Siemens, Philips and Alcatel Alsthom.
But as the dust settled, the key European players shook themselves down and were posting share gains on Thursday, enjoying the benefits of Motorola's falling market share.

"Motorola's market share is being picked off by the likes of Ericsson and Nokia so it seems in the short term if anything it could good news for the Europeans," said Morgan Stanley analyst Angela Dean.
"But the longer term is not clear as it depends on how Motorola reacts to the second year of losing market share and on new entrants to the market, including Far East players."
Ericsson rose five crowns to 164 Swedish crowns during the day's trade and Nokia gained two to 189 markka.
Analysts said Motorola's current problems in the mobile phone sector were limited to the U.S. giant.
"Motorola simply has not had the products available and has lost out in Japan where the market has been booming," Schroeder analyst Susan Anthony told Reuters.
"It has also lost out in the GSM (Global System for Mobile communications) market with only one product.
"Initially when you see something from Motorola you get a knee-jerk reaction but when people stop and think about it they realise this isn't a sector problem. It's a Motorola problem."

Finnish mobile phone giant Nokia, which ranks second in the world after Motorola and leads the European pack, has stressed that the forces affecting Motorola in the U.S. analogue market are very different from those in Europe.

"Both our volume growth as well as the trend in our inventory, in our costs and in our profitability in the second quarter indicate very clearly that we are on a somewhat different trend than some of our competitors," Nokia chief executive Jorma Ollila said last month.
Swedish telecoms major Ericsson, third in the world list, reported increasing mobile phone sales when it posted its figures for the first half of 1996 last month.
Analysts said if anythying Motorola's weak outlook and potential price cuts could benefit Ericsson.
"Ericsson buys components and if now Motorola signals lower prices the reaction should be positive," an analyst said.

Analyst Peter Knox of UBS said the short term looked bright but Motorola's problems could add to the increased competition that is building up in the sector, particularly from relative newcomers like Alcatel, Siemen and Philips.
They could take some of the market share from the three leaders Motorola, Nokia and Ericsson, who currently hold about 75 percent of the market.

"Over the long term the big three's hold of the market will come under pressure and those companies with less exposure to the handset business and better exposure to infrastructure will be better placed," Knox told Reuters.
"Whether we'll see long term earnings growth of 20-25 percent is debatable and we really should be looking at low teens. It's a function as the mobile business coming of age."
Siemens and Philips, which began mobile phone production nine months ago, shrugged off Motorola's woes.
Philips Consumer Communications president Mike McTighe said his company expected fierce competition.
"But price falls in digital cellular phones, which are Philips' main focus, are not exceeding our forecasts by much. It's no reason for us to panic," he said.
A spokesman for Siemens said Motorola's problems "have nothing to do with us" and output was increasing in terms of the number of telephones and profit in the sector rising.
